section.heading: 16.2. Line Integrals
section.paragraph: In this section we define an integral that is similar to a single integral except that instead of integrating over an interval $$\left\lbrack {a,b} \right\rbrack$$ , we integrate over a curve $$C$$ . Such integrals are called line integrals, although “curve integrals” would be better terminology. They were invented in the early 19th century to solve problems involving fluid flow, forces, electricity, and magnetism.
section.heading: Line Integrals in the Plane
section.paragraph: We start with a plane curve $$C$$ given by the parametric equations
$$x = x(t) y = y(t) a \leqslant t \leqslant b$$

or, equivalently, by the vector equation $$\mathbf{r}(t) = x(t)\mathbf{i} + y(t)\mathbf{j}$$ , and we assume that $$C$$ is a smooth curve. [This means that $$\mathbf{r}^{\prime}$$ is continuous and $$\mathbf{r}^{\prime}(t) \neq 0$$ . See Section 13.3.] If we divide the parameter interval $$\left\lbrack {a,b} \right\rbrack$$ into $$n$$ subintervals $$\left\lbrack {t_{i - 1},t_{i}} \right\rbrack$$ of equal width and we let $$x_{i} = x\left( t_{i} \right)$$ and $$y_{i} = y\left( t_{i} \right)$$ , then the corresponding points $$P_{i}\left( {x_{i},y_{i}} \right)$$ divide $$C$$ into $$n$$ subarcs with lengths $$\Delta s_{1},\Delta s_{2},\ldots,\Delta s_{n}$$ . (See Figure 1.) We choose any point $$P_{i}^{\ast}\left( {x_{i}^{\ast},y_{i}^{\ast}} \right)$$ in the ith subarc. (This corresponds to a point $$t_{i}^{\ast}$$ in $$\left\lbrack {t_{i - 1},t_{i}} \right\rbrack$$ .) Now if $$f$$ is any function of two variables whose domain includes the curve $$C$$ , we evaluate $$f$$ at the point $$\left( {x_{i}^{\ast},y_{i}^{\ast}} \right)$$ , multiply by the length $$\Delta s_{i}$$ of the subarc, and form the sum
$$\sum\limits_{i = 1}^{n}{f\left( {x_{i}^{\ast},y_{i}^{\ast}} \right)\Delta s_{i}}$$
which is similar to a Riemann sum. Then we take the limit of these sums and make the following definition by analogy with a single integral.

note.paragraph: If $$f$$ is defined on a smooth curve $$C$$ given by Equations 1, then the line integral of $$\mathbf{f}$$ along $$\mathbf{C}$$ is

section.paragraph: In Section 10.2 we found that the length of $$C$$ is
$$L = {\int_{a}^{b}{\sqrt{\left( \frac{dx}{dt} \right)^{2} + \left( \frac{dy}{dt} \right)^{2}}dt}}$$

A similar type of argument can be used to show that if $$f$$ is a continuous function, then the limit in Definition 2 always exists and the following formula can be used to evaluate the line integral:
$$\int_{C}{f\left( {x,y} \right)ds = {\int_{a}^{b}{f\left( {x(t),y(t)} \right)\sqrt{\left( \frac{dx}{dt} \right)^{2} + \left( \frac{dy}{dt} \right)^{2}}dt}}}$$
The value of the line integral does not depend on the parametrization of the curve, provided that the curve is traversed exactly once as $$t$$ increases from $$a$$ to $$b$$ .
If $$s(t)$$ is the length of $$C$$ between $$\mathbf{r}(a)$$ and $$\mathbf{r}(t)$$ , then
$$\frac{ds}{dt} = |r^{'}(t)| = \sqrt{\left( \frac{dx}{dt} \right)^{2} + \left( \frac{dy}{dt} \right)^{2}}$$
The arc length function $$s$$ is discussed in Section 13.3.

(See Equation 13.3.7.) So the way to remember Formula 3 is to express everything in terms of the parameter $$t$$ : use the parametric equations to express $$x$$ and $$y$$ in terms of $$t$$ and write $$ds$$ as
$$ds = \sqrt{\left( \frac{dx}{dt} \right)^{2} + \left( \frac{dy}{dt} \right)^{2}}dt$$

note.title: Note
note.heading: Note
note.paragraph: In the special case where $$C$$ is the line segment that joins $$\left( {a,0} \right)$$ to $$\left( {b,0} \right)$$ , using $$x$$ as the parameter, we can write the parametric equations of $$C$$ as follows: $$x = x$$ , $$y = 0$$ , $$a \leqslant x \leqslant b$$ . Formula 3 then becomes
and so the line integral reduces to an ordinary single integral in this case.

section.paragraph: Just as for an ordinary single integral, we can interpret the line integral of a positive function as an area. In fact, if $$f\left( {x,y} \right) \geqslant 0$$ , $$\int_{C}{f\left( {x,y} \right)ds}$$ represents the area of one side of the “fence” or “curtain” in Figure 2, whose base is $$C$$ and whose height above the point $$\left( {x,y} \right)$$ is $$f\left( {x,y} \right)$$ .

section.paragraph: Suppose now that $$C$$ is a piecewise-smooth curve; that is, $$C$$ is a union of a finite number of smooth curves $$C_{1},C_{2},\ldots,C_{n}$$ , where, as illustrated in Figure 4, the initial point of $$C_{i + 1}$$ is the terminal point of $$C_{i}$$ . Then we define the integral of $$f$$ along $$C$$ as the sum of the integrals of $$f$$ along each of the smooth pieces of $$C$$ :
$$\int_{C}{f\left( {x,y} \right)ds = {\int_{C_{1}}{f\left( {x,y} \right)ds + {\int_{C_{2}}{f\left( {x,y} \right)ds + \cdot \cdot \cdot + {\int_{C_{n}}{f\left( {x,y} \right)ds}}}}}}}$$

section.paragraph: Any physical interpretation of a line integral $$\int_{C}f\left( {x,y} \right)ds$$ depends on the physical interpretation of the function $$f$$ . Suppose that $$\rho\left( {x,y} \right)$$ represents the linear density at a point $$\left( {x,y} \right)$$ of a thin wire shaped like a curve $$C$$ (see Example 3.7.2). Then the mass of the part of the wire from $$P_{i - 1}$$ to $$P_{i}$$ in Figure 1 is approximately $$\rho\left( {x_{i}^{\ast},y_{i}^{\ast}} \right)\Delta s_{i}$$ and so the total mass of the wire is approximately $$\sum\rho\left( {x_{i}^{\ast},y_{i}^{\ast}} \right)\Delta s_{i}$$ . By taking more and more points on the curve, we obtain the mass $$m$$ of the wire as the limiting value of these approximations:
$$m = \lim\limits_{n\rightarrow\infty}\sum\limits_{i = 1}^{n}{\rho\left( {x_{i}^{*},y_{i}^{*}} \right)\Delta s_{i} = {\int_{C}{\rho\left( {x,y} \right)ds}}}$$

[For example, if $$f\left( {x,y} \right) = 2 + x^{2}y$$ represents the density of a semicircular wire, then the integral in Example 1 would represent the mass of the wire.] The center of mass of the wire with density function $$\rho$$ is located at the point $$\left( {\overline{x},\overline{y}} \right)$$ , where
$$\overline{x} = \frac{1}{m}{\int_{C}{x\rho\left( {x,y} \right)ds}} \overline{y} = \frac{1}{m}{\int_{C}{y\rho\left( {x,y} \right)ds}}$$
Other physical interpretations of line integrals will be discussed later in this chapter.

section.heading: Line Integrals with Respect to x or y
section.paragraph: Two other types of line integrals are obtained by replacing $$\Delta s_{i}$$ by either $$\Delta x_{i} = x_{i} - x_{i - 1}$$ or $$\Delta y_{i} = y_{i} - y_{i - 1}$$ in Definition 2. They are called the line integrals of $$f$$ along $$C$$ with respect to $$x$$ and $$y$$ :
$${\int_{C}{f\left( {x,y} \right)dx =}}\lim\limits_{n\rightarrow\infty}\sum\limits_{i = 1}^{n}{f\left( {x_{i}^{\ast},y_{i}^{\ast}} \right)\Delta x_{i}}$$
$${\int_{C}{f\left( {x,y} \right)dy =}}\lim\limits_{n\rightarrow\infty}\sum\limits_{i = 1}^{n}{f\left( {x_{i}^{\ast},y_{i}^{\ast}} \right)\Delta y_{i}}$$
When we want to distinguish the original line integral $$\int_{C}{f\left( {x,y} \right)ds}$$ from those in Equations 5 and 6, we call it the line integral with respect to arc length.

The following formulas say that line integrals with respect to $$x$$ and $$y$$ can also be evaluated by expressing everything in terms of $$t$$ : $$x = x{(t)}$$ , $$y = y{(t)}$$ , $$dx = x^{\prime}{(t)}dt$$ , $$dy = y^{\prime}{(t)}dt$$ .

We will see throughout this chapter that line integrals with respect to $$x$$ and $$y$$ frequently occur together (see, for instance, Equation 14). When this happens, it’s customary to abbreviate by writing
$$\int_{C}{P\left( {x,y} \right)dx + {\int_{C}{Q\left( {x,y} \right)dy = {\int_{C}{P\left( {x,y} \right)dx + Q\left( {x,y} \right)dy}}}}}$$

When we are setting up a line integral, sometimes the most difficult thing is to think of a parametric representation for a curve whose geometric description is given. In particular, we often need to parametrize a line segment, so it’s useful to remember that a vector representation of the line segment that starts at $$\mathbf{r}_{0}$$ and ends at $$\mathbf{r}_{1}$$ is given by
$$\mathbf{r}(t) = \left( {1 - t} \right)\mathbf{r}_{0} + t\mathbf{r}_{1} 0 \leqslant t \leqslant 1$$
(See Equation 12.5.4.)

Thus, in general, the value of a line integral depends not just on the endpoints of the curve but also on the path. (But see Section 16.3 for conditions under which the integral is independent of the path.)

section.paragraph: If $$- C$$ denotes the curve consisting of the same points as $$C$$ but with the opposite orientation (from initial point $$B$$ to terminal point $$A$$ in Figure 8), then we have
$${\int_{- C}{f\left( {x,y} \right)dx = - {\int_{C}{f\left( {x,y} \right)dx}}}} {\int_{- C}{f\left( {x,y} \right)dy = - {\int_{C}{f\left( {x,y} \right)dy}}}}$$
But if we integrate with respect to arc length, the value of the line integral does not change when we reverse the orientation of the curve:
$$\int_{- C}{f\left( {x,y} \right)ds = {\int_{C}{f\left( {x,y} \right)ds}}}$$
This is because $$\Delta s_{i}$$ is always positive, whereas $$\Delta x_{i}$$ and $$\Delta y_{i}$$ change sign when we reverse the orientation of $$C$$ .
section.heading: Line Integrals in Space
section.paragraph: We now suppose that $$C$$ is a smooth space curve given by the parametric equations
$$x = x(t)y = y(t)z = z(t)a \leqslant t \leqslant b$$

or by a vector equation $$\mathbf{r}(t) = x(t)\mathbf{i} + y(t)\mathbf{j} + z(t)\mathbf{k}$$ . If $$f$$ is a function of three variables that is continuous on some region containing $$C$$ , then we define the line integral of $$f$$ along $$\mathbf{C}$$ (with respect to arc length) in a manner similar to that for plane curves:
$$\int_{C}{f\left( {x,y,z} \right)ds = \lim\limits_{n\rightarrow\infty}\sum\limits_{i = 1}^{n}{f\left( {x_{i}^{\ast},y_{i}^{\ast},z_{i}^{\ast}} \right)\Delta s_{i}}}$$
We evaluate it using a formula similar to Formula 3:

$$\int_{C}{f\left( {x,y,z} \right)ds = {\int_{a}^{b}{f\left( {x(t),y(t),z(t)} \right)\sqrt{\left( \frac{dx}{dt} \right)^{2} + \left( \frac{dy}{dt} \right)^{2} + \left( \frac{dz}{dt} \right)^{2}}dt}}}$$
Observe that the integrals in both Formulas 3 and 9 can be written in the more compact vector notation
$$\int_{a}^{b}{f\left( {\mathbf{r}(t)} \right)\left| {\mathbf{r}^{\prime}(t)} \middle| \right.dt}$$
For the special case $$f\left( {x,y,z} \right) = 1$$ , we get
$$\int_{C}{ds = {\int_{a}^{b}{\left| {\mathbf{r}^{\prime}(t)} \middle| \right.dt = L}}}$$
where $$L$$ is the length of the curve $$C$$ (see Formula 13.3.3).
Line integrals along $$C$$ with respect to $$x$$ , $$y$$ , and $$z$$ can also be defined. For example,

$$\begin{array}{l} {\int_{C}{f\left( {x,y,z} \right)dz = \lim\limits_{n\rightarrow\infty}{\sum\limits_{i = 1}^{n}{f\left( {x_{i}^{\ast},y_{i}^{\ast},z_{i}^{\ast}} \right)\Delta z_{i}}}}} \\ {\phantom{\int_{C}{f\left( {x,y,z} \right)dz}} = {\int_{a}^{b}{f\left( {x(t),y(t),z(t)} \right)z^{\prime}(t)dt}}} \end{array}$$
Therefore, as with line integrals in the plane, we evaluate integrals of the form
$$\int_{C}{P\left( {x,y,z} \right)dx + Q\left( {x,y,z} \right)dy + R\left( {x,y,z} \right)dz}$$
by expressing everything $$\left( x \right.,y,z,{dx},{dy},\left. {dz} \right)$$ in terms of the parameter $$t$$ .

section.heading: Line Integrals of Vector Fields; Work
section.paragraph: Recall from Section 6.4 that the work done by a variable force $$f(x)$$ in moving a particle from $$a$$ to $$b$$ along the $$x$$ -axis is $$W = {\int_{a}^{b}{f(x)dx}}$$ . Then in Section 12.3 we found that the work done by a constant force $$\mathbf{F}$$ in moving an object from a point $$P$$ to another point $$Q$$ in space is $$W = \mathbf{F} \cdot \mathbf{D}$$ , where $$\mathbf{D} = \overset{\rightarrow}{PQ}$$ is the displacement vector.

Now suppose that $$\mathbf{F} = P\mathbf{i} + Q\mathbf{j} + R\mathbf{k}$$ is a continuous force field on $${\mathbb{R}}^{3}$$ , such as the gravitational field of Example 16.1.4 or the electric force field of Example 16.1.5. (A force field on $${\mathbb{R}}^{2}$$ could be regarded as a special case where $$R = 0$$ and $$P$$ and $$Q$$ depend only on $$x$$ and $$y$$ .) We wish to compute the work done by this force in moving a particle along a smooth curve $$C$$ . See Figure 11.

image.alt: Details A force field and a curve are graphed in the first octant of the x y z coordinate space. The positive x-axis slopes down and to the left. The positive y axis slopes slightly down and to the right. The positive z axis runs vertically upward. The vectors are longer at the front and bottom and shorter at the back and top. They are oriented along a curved path going up and to the back, concave up. The curve, labeled C, resembles an arch, begins from a point at the front, goes up to the right and back, concave down, reaches a high point, and then goes down to the right and back, until another marked point. An arrowhead placed on the curve points clockwise. A single arrow, tangent to the curve, near the highpoint, is in bold.

section.paragraph: To find the work done by $$\mathbf{F}$$ in moving a particle along $$C$$ , we divide $$C$$ into subarcs $$P_{i - 1}P_{i}$$ with lengths $$\Delta s_{i}$$ by dividing the parameter interval $$\left\lbrack {a,b} \right\rbrack$$ into subintervals of equal width. (See Figure 1 for the two-dimensional case or Figure 12 for the three-dimensional case.) Choose a point $$P_{i}^{\ast}\left( {x_{i}^{\ast},y_{i}^{\ast},z_{i}^{\ast}} \right)$$ on the $$i$$ th subarc corresponding to the parameter value $$t_{i}^{\ast}$$ . If $$\Delta s_{i}$$ is small, then as the particle moves from $$P_{i - 1}$$ to $$P_{i}$$ along the curve, it proceeds approximately in the direction of $$\mathbf{T}\left( t_{i}^{\ast} \right)$$ , the unit tangent vector at $$P_{i}^{\ast}$$ . Thus the work done by the force $$\mathbf{F}$$ in moving the particle from $$P_{i - 1}$$ to $$P_{i}$$ is approximately

$$\mathbf{F}\left( {x_{i}^{\ast},y_{i}^{\ast},z_{i}^{\ast}} \right) \cdot \left\lbrack {\Delta s_{i}\mathbf{T}\left( t_{i}^{\ast} \right)} \right\rbrack = \left\lbrack {\mathbf{F}\left( {x_{i}^{\ast},y_{i}^{\ast},z_{i}^{\ast}} \right) \cdot \mathbf{T}\left( t_{i}^{\ast} \right)} \right\rbrack\Delta s_{i}$$
and the total work done in moving the particle along $$C$$ is approximately

$$\sum\limits_{i = 1}^{n}{\left\lbrack {\mathbf{F}\left( {x_{i}^{\ast},y_{i}^{\ast},z_{i}^{\ast}} \right) \cdot \mathbf{T}\left( {x_{i}^{\ast},y_{i}^{\ast},z_{i}^{\ast}} \right)} \right\rbrack\Delta s_{i}}$$

where $$\mathbf{T}\left( {x,y,z} \right)$$ is the unit tangent vector at the point $$\left( {x,y,z} \right)$$ on $$C$$ . Intuitively, we see that these approximations ought to become better as $$n$$ becomes larger. Therefore we define the work $$W$$ done by the force field $$\mathbf{F}$$ as the limit of the Riemann sums in (11), namely,
$$W = {\int_{C}{\mathbf{F}\left( {x,y,z} \right) \cdot \mathbf{T}\left( {x,y,z} \right)ds = {\int_{C}{\mathbf{F} \cdot \mathbf{T}ds}}}}$$
Equation 12 says that work is the line integral with respect to arc length of the tangential component of the force.

section.paragraph: If the curve $$C$$ is given by the vector equation $$\mathbf{r}(t) = x(t)\mathbf{i} + y(t)\mathbf{j} + z(t)\mathbf{k}$$ , then $$\mathbf{T}(t) = \mathbf{r}^{\prime}(t) \slash \left| {\mathbf{r}^{\prime}(t)} \right|$$ , so using Equation 9 we can rewrite Equation 12 in the form

$$W = {\int_{a}^{b}{\left\lbrack {\mathbf{F}\left( {\mathbf{r}(t)} \right) \cdot \frac{\mathbf{r}^{\prime}(t)}{\left| {\mathbf{r}^{\prime}(t)} \right|}} \right\rbrack\left| {\mathbf{r}^{\prime}(t)} \right|dt}} = {\int_{a}^{b}{\mathbf{F}\left( {\mathbf{r}(t)} \right) \cdot \mathbf{r}^{\prime}(t)dt}}$$

This integral is often abbreviated as $$\int_{C}{\mathbf{F} \cdot d\mathbf{r}}$$ and occurs in other areas of physics as well. Therefore we make the following definition for the line integral of any continuous vector field.

section.paragraph: Finally, we note the connection between line integrals of vector fields and line integrals of scalar fields. Suppose the vector field $$\mathbf{F}$$ on $${\mathbb{R}}^{3}$$ is given in component form by the equation $$\mathbf{F} = P\mathbf{i} + Q\mathbf{j} + R\mathbf{k}$$ . We use Definition 13 to compute its line integral along $$C$$ :

$$\begin{matrix} {{\int_{C}{\mathbf{F} \cdot d\mathbf{r}}} = {\int_{a}^{b}{\mathbf{F}\left( {\mathbf{r}(t)} \right) \cdot \mathbf{r}^{\prime}(t)dt}}} \\ {\phantom{\int_{C}{\mathbf{F} \cdot d\mathbf{r}}} = {\int_{a}^{b}{\left( {P\mathbf{i} + Q\mathbf{j} + R\mathbf{k}} \right) \cdot \left( {x^{\prime}(t)\mathbf{i} + y^{\prime}(t)\mathbf{j} + z^{\prime}(t)\mathbf{k}} \right)dt}}} \\ {\phantom{\int_{C}{\mathbf{F} \cdot d\mathbf{r}}} = {\int_{a}^{b}\lbrack P\left( {x(t),y(t),z(t)} \right)x^{\prime}(t) + Q\left( {x(t),y(t),z(t)} \right)y^{\prime}(t)}} \\ {{\left. + R\left( {x(t),y(t),z(t)} \right)z^{\prime}(t) \right\rbrack dt}} \end{matrix}$$
But this last integral is precisely the line integral in (10). Therefore we have
$${\int_{C}{\mathbf{F} \cdot d\mathbf{r} = {\int_{C}{Pdx + Qdy + Rdz}}}} {where}\mathbf{F} = P\mathbf{i} + Q\mathbf{j} + R\mathbf{k}$$
For example, the integral $$\int_{C}{ydx + zdy + xdz}$$ in Example 6 could be expressed as $$\int_{C}{\mathbf{F} \cdot d\mathbf{r}}$$ , where
$$\mathbf{F}\left( {x,y,z} \right) = y\mathbf{i} + z\mathbf{j} + x\mathbf{k}$$
A similar result holds for vector fields $$\mathbf{F}$$ on $${\mathbb{R}}^{2}$$ :
$$\int_{C}\mathbf{F} \cdot d\mathbf{r} = \int_{C}Pdx + Qdy$$
where $$\mathbf{F} = P\mathbf{i} + Q\mathbf{j}$$ .
